strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and real limitation of MBRL: L2 reconstruction losses in visually complex environments can miss small but decision-critical objects, and the paper provides clear qualitative evidence of this (Appendix B) as well as quantitative evidence via the reconstruction decoding experiment (Section 5.1).

The pipeline is a sensible, practical integration of a modern pretrained video object segmentation model (Cutie) into a strong existing MBRL backbone (STORM), avoiding reliance on privileged game states or extensive labeling, which distinguishes it from several prior object-centric RL approaches.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three domains (Atari 100k with 26 games, a custom Hollow Knight boss-fight benchmark, and Meta-world continuous control tasks in the appendix), which is unusually broad for this kind of paper.

Thorough set of ablation studies: object vector vs. mask representation (vs. FOCUS-style masks), MLP vs. attention-based policy heads, number of annotation frames needed, and robustness to simulated segmentation failures -- these give useful insight into design choices.
Transparent discussion of limitations (duplicated instances, background-relevant information not captured by objects) with concrete illustrative failure cases (Appendix H).

Good engineering effort and documentation for building a nontrivial Hollow Knight RL environment (custom reward shaping analysis, action space design, infrastructure for windowed game interaction), which could be a useful resource/benchmark for the community.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility material: full hyperparameters, loss functions, and annotation examples in the appendix.
weaknesses: Overall Atari improvement is modest and mixed: OC-STORM outperforms the re-run baseline (STORM*) on only 18/26 games, and the median HNS improvement (43.8% vs 42.5%) is marginal despite the added complexity and privileged per-game object annotations; comparison to originally published STORM numbers (122% mean, 42% median) further suggests the gain from this added machinery is not dramatic in aggregate.

The method fundamentally depends on manual, environment-specific segmentation annotations (6-12 frames per game/boss) and a predetermined, fixed object count K per environment, which limits the generality/scalability claims and reintroduces a form of human/domain-specific engineering that other 'general agent' baselines do not require.

The Hollow Knight benchmark is entirely custom (non-standardized reward shaping, action space, FPS, and boss selection), making the comparisons with baseline STORM largely self-contained; comparisons to other published Hollow Knight RL methods are explicitly acknowledged as unfair, weakening the significance of the Hollow Knight results as external validation.
Limited seeds for Hollow Knight (3 seeds) reduce statistical confidence in the reported improvements, especially for close results (e.g., Pure Vessel win rates near 0%).

No analysis of the added computational/wall-clock cost of running Cutie during data collection, nor of total pipeline latency, which is relevant for a paper motivated partly by improving practical sample/compute efficiency.

The core technical contribution is primarily an engineering/systems integration of an existing pretrained segmentation model with an existing world model architecture rather than a new algorithmic or theoretical advance, which somewhat limits novelty for a top-tier venue.

Structural limitations acknowledged by the authors (duplicate objects, non-object background information such as terrain/tunnels) are fairly fundamental to many real-world and game scenarios, and no concrete solution or mitigation is proposed beyond flagging them as future work.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and real limitation of L2/reconstruction-based world models: they can be dominated by large/static background regions and fail to capture small, decision-relevant objects.

Practical, relatively lightweight integration of a frozen pretrained video segmentation foundation model (Cutie) into an MBRL pipeline, avoiding costly end-to-end object-discovery training used by prior unsupervised slot-based methods.

Extensive ablation studies: vector vs. mask object representation (Sec 5.2), MLP vs. attention-based policy (App E.1), number of annotation labels needed (App E.2), robustness to simulated segmentation failures (App K), and an additional Meta-world evaluation against MWM/DreamerV2 (App J) that broadens the evidence base.

Introduces and open-source-documents a nontrivial custom Hollow Knight RL environment/infrastructure (modding plugin, VM-based interaction, custom reward/action space design), which could be a useful community resource for a harder visual benchmark.

Reasonably careful experimental hygiene: re-running the STORM baseline (STORM*) under an identical codebase/config for fair comparison, multiple seeds, and thorough hyperparameter/appendix documentation supporting reproducibility.

Qualitative analysis (Fig. 3, 5, 6) provides some support that object feature vectors retain sufficient state/position information and that baseline reconstruction genuinely misses key characters in Hollow Knight.
weaknesses: The headline Atari 100k results are mixed: while mean HNS improves over the re-run baseline (134.8% vs 114.2%), the median HNS is essentially flat or worse than prior methods (43.8% vs DreamerV3's 49% and STORM's 42%), suggesting gains are concentrated in a handful of games rather than broadly distributed, and DIAMOND's mean (146%) still exceeds OC-STORM's.

By the authors' own categorization, OC-STORM actually underperforms the baseline in games where not all key information can be represented as objects (124.0% vs 130.0% for STORM*), which is close to a tautological result (object-centric methods help only when objects are exactly what's decision relevant) and limits the generality of the claimed contribution.

The method fundamentally requires hand-annotating 6–12 segmentation masks per environment/boss with prior knowledge of which objects matter, which the paper argues is acceptable but nonetheless undercuts claims of general applicability to arbitrary/visually complex environments without domain-specific engineering.

Technical novelty is largely a systems/integration contribution (combining an existing pretrained tracker, Cutie, with an existing MBRL backbone, STORM) rather than a new algorithmic idea; the spatial-temporal transformer and VAE components are directly inherited from STORM/DreamerV3 with only object-token additions.

The Hollow Knight evaluation, while interesting, is on a non-standardized, self-built benchmark; the paper explicitly acknowledges that comparison with prior Hollow Knight RL work (Yang, 2023) is 'not necessarily a fair comparison,' weakening the claim of achieving 'best-known sample efficiency' on this domain.

Known and substantial limitations are acknowledged but unresolved: Cutie fails on duplicate/identical objects (e.g., Mantis Lords, MsPacman beans) and cannot represent important non-object background structures (e.g., Gopher's tunnel), both of which can silently degrade performance without clear mitigation beyond noting them as future work.

Statistical robustness is somewhat limited for Atari 100k standards (5 seeds) and especially for Hollow Knight (3 seeds), given the well-known high variance of these benchmarks, making some game-level or boss-level comparisons (e.g., single-percentage-point win-rate differences) less conclusive.

strengths: Clear motivation grounded in a concrete empirical demonstration (Section 5.1/Appendix B) that standard L2-reconstruction MBRL (STORM) fails to reconstruct small/decision-critical objects in visually complex scenes like Hollow Knight, well illustrating the paper's core hypothesis.

The proposed pipeline is simple, modular, and practically integrable with existing state-of-the-art MBRL (STORM), using a frozen pre-trained segmentation/tracking model (Cutie) rather than requiring costly end-to-end training of an object detector, which is a pragmatic engineering choice.

Extensive empirical evaluation: full Atari 100k benchmark (26 games, 5 seeds), a novel and substantially more visually complex benchmark (Hollow Knight bosses), and additional Meta-world continuous-control experiments in the appendix, showing the approach generalizes beyond simple 2D games.

Thorough set of ablation studies: vector vs. mask object representation, attention-based vs. MLP-based policy heads, number of annotation labels needed, and robustness to simulated segmentation failures (random zeroing of object features) — these add good empirical rigor and transparency.

Honest and thoughtful discussion of limitations (duplicated instances, background/non-object information) with illustrative failure-case figures, which strengthens the credibility of the work rather than overselling it.

Nontrivial systems/engineering contribution in building a working Hollow Knight RL environment (reward signal via a game mod, screen capture pipeline, background execution via Hyper-V) that could be a useful resource for the community.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility materials (full loss functions, hyperparameters, annotation counts, and inputs used) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The method still requires hand-annotating several segmentation masks per environment/boss (6 for Atari, 12 for Hollow Knight) and manually specifying the number/identity of objects per game, which limits the approach's autonomy and general applicability compared to fully self-supervised MBRL.

Overall gains on Atari 100k are mixed: while the mean HNS improves, the median HNS improvement is marginal (42.5% to 43.8%), and for the 'not fully object-representable' category of games OC-STORM actually underperforms the baseline, suggesting the benefits are narrow and environment-dependent.

The STORM* baseline used for direct comparison is re-run with a 'more lightweight configuration' that differs from the original published STORM, which could complicate fair comparison and slightly muddies the credit assignment for observed gains.

Hollow Knight results cannot be rigorously compared against prior model-free approaches due to differing reward schemes, action spaces, and sample budgets (acknowledged by the authors), limiting the strength of claims about 'best-known sample efficiency' on this benchmark.

No direct quantitative comparison to the most similar prior work (FOCUS) or other object-centric baselines (e.g., OC-SA/Nakano et al.) on the same benchmarks, only qualitative/discussion-level differentiation.

The core algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental — it is largely a combination of an existing off-the-shelf video segmentation model (Cutie) with an existing MBRL backbone (STORM), rather than a fundamentally new modeling technique, which may limit its impact/significance for a top-tier venue.

The duplicated-instance limitation (e.g., multiple similar enemies) is a substantive weakness that could affect many practical visually complex environments beyond the specific examples shown, and is left entirely as future work.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practical limitation of pixel-reconstruction-based MBRL (small task-critical objects being ignored), with clear illustrative evidence (Figure 1).

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple axes: two world-model backbones (STORM, DreamerV3), two segmentation models (Cutie, SAM2), two representation types (vector vs mask), 26 Atari games, 6 Hollow Knight bosses, and 4 Meta-World tasks.

Introduces a novel and more visually complex/dynamic testbed (Hollow Knight boss fights) for OCRL/MBRL beyond the well-worn Atari benchmark, along with a custom environment wrapper, reward shaping analysis, and action-space design, which could be a useful resource for the community.

Thorough ablation studies (number of annotations, segmentation failure robustness via feature zeroing, missing-object ablations, attention vs MLP policy, computational overhead) that provide practical insights beyond just the headline results.

Reasonable, low-cost approach (few-shot annotation with frozen pretrained segmentation models) avoiding privileged state information, which is more practical than approaches requiring internal game state or heavy annotation.
Transparent discussion of limitations (duplicated instances, geometric/map representations) and honest acknowledgment that Hollow Knight comparisons to prior work are not strictly fair.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it largely combines existing pretrained segmentation/tracking models (Cutie/SAM2) with an existing world-model backbone (STORM/DreamerV3) via a fairly straightforward token-fusion architecture; the main novelty is engineering integration rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea.

Improvements on Atari 100k (HNS mean 134.8% vs comparable baselines like DIAMOND 145.9%, Table 2) are not uniformly state-of-the-art, and median HNS (43.8%) is notably lower than several baselines (e.g., IRIS median... TWM 50.5%, DIAMOND is lower too but overall mean claims of 'state-of-the-art sample efficiency' are overstated given mixed results across metrics/baselines.

Requiring manual object annotation and a user-specified, environment-specific K (number of objects) reduces the 'general applicability' claimed; this is a form of light supervision/prior knowledge that is not discussed quantitatively as a cost trade-off against baselines that need none.

Hollow Knight results, the paper's flagship complex-domain claim, are only compared against the authors' own STORM baseline (with different reward shaping and action space than prior work), not against a fair or controlled external baseline; the comparison to Yang (2023) is explicitly stated as 'not strictly fair,' undermining the strength of the 'state-of-the-art' claim in this domain.

Statistical rigor is limited: Atari results use 5 seeds and Hollow Knight only 3 seeds, and no significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the main comparison tables, making it hard to assess whether improvements are robust versus noise, especially given typical high variance in Atari 100k results.

The categorization into 'Obj-detectable' vs 'Otherwise' games (used to justify the method's benefits) is done post-hoc by the authors themselves based on their own segmentation model's performance, which risks selection bias in framing the narrative of when the method helps.

The paper does not clearly quantify the annotation cost/human effort trade-off (e.g., time to annotate 6-12 masks per game) or scalability to environments with many/dynamic object counts, given the noted 'duplicated instances' and fixed-K limitations.

Presentation is dense with many appendices; the main paper's Table 1 is complex and could benefit from clearer statistical treatment (e.g., variance bars) to substantiate the highlighted differences between very close scores (e.g., 5% bolding threshold may mask true significance).

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple axes: two world-model backbones (STORM, DreamerV3), two segmentation extractors (Cutie, SAM2), two representation types (vector vs. mask), and three domains (Atari 100k, Hollow Knight, Meta-world).

Substantial engineering effort to build a working Hollow Knight RL testbed (custom screen-capture/keyboard wrapper, modding plugin for reward signals, VM-based background execution), which could be a useful resource if released.

A reasonably thorough set of ablations (missing-object ablation, robustness to simulated segmentation failures via feature zeroing, number of annotations, attention- vs MLP-based policy, computational overhead) that provide some mechanistic insight into why the method works.

Honest discussion of limitations (duplicated-instance tracking failures, inability to represent geometric/navigable structures) and explicit acknowledgment that Hollow Knight comparisons to prior work are not strictly fair.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an engineering integration of existing off-the-shelf components (Cutie/SAM2 features + STORM/DreamerV3 latent dynamics), with limited genuinely new modeling ideas beyond a spatial-temporal token fusion scheme; novelty over prior OC-RL/world-model work (e.g., FOCUS, OCAtari, Nakano et al.) is incremental.

The 'state-of-the-art sample efficiency' claim is not well supported: in Table 2, DIAMOND achieves a higher mean HNS (145.9% vs. 134.8%) and comparable/better median HNS than OC-STORM on Atari 100k, so the method is only clearly SOTA relative to its own STORM baseline, not to the field.

Requiring 6-12 hand-annotated frames per game/boss with a manually chosen, environment-specific number of objects K undercuts the 'without extensive labeling' framing; this is domain knowledge injection tailored per-task rather than a general-purpose, label-free solution, and no systematic annotation-cost-vs-benefit analysis appears in the main text.

Table 1 shows a stark asymmetry between 'Obj-detectable' (186.2%) and 'Otherwise' (83.4%) categories, indicating the benefit is highly non-uniform and largely confined to games where the authors could hand-pick cleanly segmentable objects — this selection itself risks confirmation bias in the evaluation design.

The Hollow Knight benchmark is entirely custom (non-public simulator, bespoke reward shaping, only 3 seeds per boss), making it difficult to reproduce or independently verify; the only external comparison (Yang, 2023) is explicitly flagged by the authors as not a fair comparison.

No error bars/statistical testing are reported for the per-game Atari scores in Table 1 despite averaging over 5 seeds, making it hard to assess whether many of the reported gains over STORM/DreamerV3 are significant given the well-known high variance of Atari 100k results.

The FOCUS mask-based baseline is not the original method but an in-house reimplementation (Cutie masks fed into STORM rather than the original TrackAnything+DreamerV2 pipeline), which may bias this comparison in the paper's favor.

The claimed practicality/generality is undermined by the reliance on frozen natural-image-pretrained segmentation models that the paper itself shows can fail on duplicated instances or unusual object states (Appendix I, F.2), with no principled solution offered beyond zeroing out failed detections.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple axes: two world model backbones (STORM, DreamerV3), two segmentation extractors (Cutie, SAM2), two representation types (vector vs. mask), and three domains (Atari 100k, Hollow Knight, MetaWorld), which gives good coverage of the design space.

Introduces a challenging, visually complex new testbed (Hollow Knight boss fights) with a custom environment wrapper, carefully designed multi-binary action space, and a well-motivated reward/termination scheme, adding practical value beyond the Atari benchmark.

Rich set of ablations and analyses: robustness to segmentation failures (zeroing features), sensitivity to number of few-shot annotations, attention-based vs. MLP policy heads, missing-object ablations, and qualitative reconstruction probes that validate that object features retain position/state information.
Honest and clearly articulated limitations section (duplicated-instance tracking failures, inability to represent geometric/navigable structures) supported by qualitative failure-case figures.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed architecture diagrams, loss functions, hyperparameter tables, and computational overhead/latency benchmarking.
Direct comparison to the most relevant prior work (FOCUS-style mask-based OC representations) showing vector-based object features are more effective and efficient.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is primarily integrative/engineering (combining off-the-shelf frozen segmentation networks with existing STORM/DreamerV3 backbones) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the core architectural change (adding an object token stream to a spatial-temporal transformer) is a relatively incremental extension of STORM.

The "state-of-the-art sample efficiency" claim is not fully supported on Atari: Table 2 shows DIAMOND achieves higher mean HNS (145.9% vs. 134.8%) and both IRIS and ∆-IRIS achieve higher median HNS than OC-STORM, so the SOTA claim needs to be scoped more carefully (e.g., to object-detectable subsets or Hollow Knight only).

Hollow Knight results rely on a fully custom, non-public simulator/environment wrapper (Windows VM + modding plugin) with only 3 seeds, and the comparison to prior model-free work (Yang, 2023) is explicitly acknowledged by the authors as not a fair/controlled comparison, limiting the strength of the sample-efficiency claims in this domain.

The method still depends on non-trivial human input: manual specification of the number of objects K per game and hand-annotation of segmentation masks (6–12 frames), which partially undercuts the framing of a broadly automatic, low-effort pipeline, especially for scaling to many new tasks.

Non-trivial computational overhead from running Cutie/SAM2 alongside the world model (training throughput drops from 8.1 it/s to 5.3–5.9 it/s, i.e., ~30-45% slower), which is understated as "acceptable" without deeper discussion of how this scales to larger annotation/object counts or longer training budgets.

Known failure modes (duplicate-instance tracking, inability to encode geometric/navigable structures) are significant for many real-world visual domains and are only partially mitigated by falling back on raw visual input, suggesting the object-centric benefit may be narrower than the broad claims in the abstract/introduction suggest.

Statistical rigor is limited: main result tables report only mean scores without confidence intervals or significance tests across the compared variants, making some of the finer-grained comparisons (e.g., SAM2- vs Cutie-based OC) harder to assess definitively.
